Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy

A sham-controlled trial in established neuropathy reported benefit, while a separate phase II sham-controlled trial found little clear advantage at measured time points. A prevention pilot and a dose-comparison trial reported selected improvements. Mouse and cell findings come from one separate publication.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A sham-controlled trial in established neuropathy reported benefit, while a separate phase II sham-controlled trial found little clear advantage at measured time points. A prevention pilot and a dose-comparison trial reported selected improvements. Mouse and cell findings come from one separate publication.

Summary of the Evidence

Ten unique titles were identified: six human primary studies, two narrative reviews, one systematic review, and one 2026 preclinical publication. The human studies comprise four randomized trials and two other studies; the preclinical paper includes both mouse and in-vitro experiments, so those tags refer to one title. The reviews summarize these primary reports and are not new cohorts. No clear human cohort overlap was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

In established chemotherapy-induced neuropathy, a 70-person double-blind crossover trial reported improvement with PBM compared with sham. A 44-person phase II sham-controlled trial found little clear PBM advantage at its measured time points. A 32-person randomized placebo-controlled prevention pilot studied PBM during chemotherapy, while the 60-person randomized NEUROLIGHT dose-comparison trial compared 6 with 8 J/cm²: pain and mobility improved, the lower dose performed better for pain, and health-related quality of life did not improve. Two other human studies were single-arm or non-randomized, so change over time cannot be attributed to PBM alone (Argenta et al. 2017 Teng et al. 2022 Lodewijckx et al. 2022 Claes et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

Ren and colleagues tested near-infrared PBM in a mouse model and reported reduced mechanical and cold hypersensitivity with preservation of peripheral nerve fibers. This is preclinical evidence and does not establish prevention or treatment in patients (Ren et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The same Ren publication included N2a neuroblastoma cells and normal human astrocytes exposed to paclitaxel with or without PBM. This is one publication with separate laboratory work, not a second animal or clinical cohort (Ren et al. 2026).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The preclinical paper used near-infrared PBM at 808 nm. Human protocols varied in timing, anatomical treatment points, wavelength, and dose; NEUROLIGHT compared 6 and 8 J/cm². These differences matter because treatment during chemotherapy for prevention is not the same question as treatment of established neuropathy.

Interpretation

Randomized human evidence supports further evaluation of selected sensory, pain, and mobility outcomes, but sham-controlled results are mixed and quality-of-life benefit is not established. The animal and cell results are supportive mechanistic evidence rather than clinical confirmation.

Evidence strength in source summaryPain and sensory symptoms in established neuropathy: Low Prevention during chemotherapy: Very low Animal sensory outcomes: Very low
Publications and records10 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Four randomized human studies include sham-controlled treatment and prevention trials, but the results differ by population, timing, dose, and outcome. Two additional human studies are uncontrolled or single-arm. One publication contributes both mouse and cell evidence, while reviews do not add cohorts. Larger independent trials with common pain, sensory, mobility, and quality-of-life measures are needed.
